title: Classical AI: Search, Reasoning & Planning
blurb: Search, heuristics, CSPs, games, logic, knowledge representation, planning, uncertainty and MDPs.
description: A certification-style classical AI foundation aligned to NPTEL/IIT search and knowledge-representation curricula, with hands-on Python models and problem-formulation practice.

lessons.title: Intelligent agents & problem formulation
objectives: Formulate a real problem as states, actions, goals, and costs.
Explain how agent changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect agent with state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Classical AI begins by choosing a representation that makes reasoning possible. An agent observes an environment and chooses actions; a search problem specifies an initial state, possible actions, transition model, goal test, and path cost.
lessons.explain: Classical AI begins by choosing a representation that makes reasoning possible. An agent observes an environment and chooses actions; a search problem specifies an initial state, possible actions, transition model, goal test, and path cost.
commonMistakes: Choosing a state representation that omits information needed for future decisions can make the correct solution impossible to express.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: State spaces, graphs & search trees
objectives: Distinguish the underlying state graph from the search tree generated by an algorithm.
Explain how state space changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect state space with search tree and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A state space is the set of possible configurations and transitions. A search tree is the algorithm’s unfolding of that space from the start state, so the same world state may appear many times through different paths.
lessons.explain: A state space is the set of possible configurations and transitions. A search tree is the algorithm’s unfolding of that space from the start state, so the same world state may appear many times through different paths.
commonMistakes: Treating every search-tree node as a new world state can cause exponential repeated work in cyclic or converging graphs.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Breadth-first & depth-first search
objectives: Choose BFS or DFS based on solution depth, memory, and completeness.
Explain how BFS changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect BFS with DFS and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Breadth-first search expands the shallowest frontier first and is complete on finite branching graphs; with equal step costs it finds a shortest path in number of edges. Depth-first search follows one branch deeply using little frontier memory but can waste time down an unhelpful path and needs cycle handling.
lessons.explain: Breadth-first search expands the shallowest frontier first and is complete on finite branching graphs; with equal step costs it finds a shortest path in number of edges. Depth-first search follows one branch deeply using little frontier memory but can waste time down an unhelpful path and needs cycle handling.
commonMistakes: Using DFS when the search space can contain an infinite branch can prevent the algorithm from ever reaching a nearby solution elsewhere.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Uniform-cost search & path cost
objectives: Find the least-cost path when actions have different costs.
Explain how uniform-cost search changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect uniform-cost search with priority queue and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Uniform-cost search expands the frontier node with the lowest accumulated path cost g(n). With non-negative step costs, the first time a goal is removed from the priority queue its cost is optimal.
lessons.explain: Uniform-cost search expands the frontier node with the lowest accumulated path cost g(n). With non-negative step costs, the first time a goal is removed from the priority queue its cost is optimal.
examples:
import heapq
frontier=[(0,"A")]
heapq.heappush(frontier,(5,"C"))
heapq.heappush(frontier,(2,"B"))
print(heapq.heappop(frontier))
lessons.example:
import heapq
frontier=[(0,"A")]
heapq.heappush(frontier,(5,"C")); heapq.heappush(frontier,(2,"B"))
print(heapq.heappop(frontier))
commonMistakes: Marking a node permanently visited when it is first generated rather than when its best cost is established can discard a cheaper path found later.

lessons.title: Heuristics & greedy best-first search
objectives: Design a heuristic and understand what information it adds to search.
Explain how heuristic changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect heuristic with greedy best-first and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost from a state to a goal. Greedy best-first search expands the state with the smallest heuristic estimate, often reaching a goal quickly but without considering the cost already paid.
lessons.explain: A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost from a state to a goal. Greedy best-first search expands the state with the smallest heuristic estimate, often reaching a goal quickly but without considering the cost already paid.
commonMistakes: A heuristic that looks intuitive but systematically overvalues the wrong feature can make informed search worse than a simpler baseline.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: A* search, admissibility & consistency
objectives: Explain why A* balances known path cost with estimated remaining cost.
Explain how A* changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect A* with admissible heuristic and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A* orders states by f(n)=g(n)+h(n), combining the cost already paid with an estimate of the cost remaining. An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost; consistency adds a triangle-inequality-style condition across edges and makes graph-search behavior cleaner.
lessons.explain: A* orders states by f(n)=g(n)+h(n), combining the cost already paid with an estimate of the cost remaining. An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost; consistency adds a triangle-inequality-style condition across edges and makes graph-search behavior cleaner.
commonMistakes: Using a heuristic because it “usually seems close” without checking its admissibility can silently remove the optimality guarantee.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Local search: hill climbing & simulated annealing
objectives: Use local search when the path is irrelevant and only a good final state matters.
Explain how hill climbing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect hill climbing with local optimum and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Local search keeps one or a small number of candidate states and improves an objective rather than constructing a path from start to goal. Hill climbing moves to a better neighbor but can become trapped on local optima, ridges, or plateaus.
lessons.explain: Local search keeps one or a small number of candidate states and improves an objective rather than constructing a path from start to goal. Hill climbing moves to a better neighbor but can become trapped on local optima, ridges, or plateaus.
lessons.example:
scores=[3,5,7,6,9]
best=scores[0]
for s in scores[1:]:
    if s>best: best=s
print("best observed",best)
commonMistakes: Assuming hill climbing found the global optimum because no immediate neighbor is better confuses local optimality with global optimality.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Constraint satisfaction & backtracking
objectives: Model a problem as variables, domains, constraints, and a systematic search.
Explain how CSP changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CSP with variable and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Constraint Satisfaction Problems separate representation from search: variables must receive values from domains while satisfying constraints. Backtracking assigns one variable at a time and reverses choices when a constraint fails.
lessons.explain: Constraint Satisfaction Problems separate representation from search: variables must receive values from domains while satisfying constraints. Backtracking assigns one variable at a time and reverses choices when a constraint fails.
examples:
colors=["R","G","B"]
solutions=[(a,b) for a in colors for b in colors if a!=b]
print(solutions)
lessons.example:
colors=["R","G","B"]
solutions=[(a,b) for a in colors for b in colors if a!=b]
print(solutions)
commonMistakes: Generating complete assignments before checking constraints throws away the main advantage of backtracking: pruning impossible partial solutions early.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Constraint propagation, MRV & arc consistency
objectives: Reduce CSP search by propagating constraints before making more guesses.
Explain how MRV changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MRV with forward checking and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Constraint propagation removes domain values that cannot participate in a valid solution. Forward checking prunes neighbors after an assignment; arc consistency repeatedly ensures each value of one variable has compatible support in a connected variable.
lessons.explain: Constraint propagation removes domain values that cannot participate in a valid solution. Forward checking prunes neighbors after an assignment; arc consistency repeatedly ensures each value of one variable has compatible support in a connected variable.
commonMistakes: Propagation must preserve only logically impossible values; over-pruning can delete valid solutions and make the solver appear fast but incorrect.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Adversarial search & minimax
objectives: Choose an action assuming an opponent also acts rationally.
Explain how minimax changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect minimax with MAX and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Adversarial search models environments where another agent actively tries to reduce your outcome. Minimax alternates MAX nodes, which choose the highest utility, and MIN nodes, which choose the lowest utility from MAX’s perspective.
lessons.explain: Adversarial search models environments where another agent actively tries to reduce your outcome. Minimax alternates MAX nodes, which choose the highest utility, and MIN nodes, which choose the lowest utility from MAX’s perspective.
commonMistakes: Evaluating only your own best next move ignores the opponent’s response and produces plans that fail immediately against rational play.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Alpha-beta pruning & evaluation functions
objectives: Prune game-tree branches that cannot affect the minimax decision.
Explain how alpha-beta pruning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect alpha-beta pruning with evaluation function and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Alpha-beta pruning computes the same minimax choice while skipping branches proven irrelevant to the final result. Alpha tracks MAX’s best guaranteed value so far; beta tracks MIN’s.
lessons.explain: Alpha-beta pruning computes the same minimax choice while skipping branches proven irrelevant to the final result. Alpha tracks MAX’s best guaranteed value so far; beta tracks MIN’s.
commonMistakes: A fast evaluation function with poor correlation to winning can make deeper search confidently choose bad moves.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Propositional logic & knowledge bases
objectives: Represent facts and rules with precise truth conditions.
Explain how proposition changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect proposition with logical connective and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Propositional logic represents statements that are true or false and combines them with NOT, AND, OR, implication, and equivalence. A knowledge base is a set of sentences; entailment asks whether every model that satisfies the knowledge base also satisfies a query.
lessons.explain: Propositional logic represents statements that are true or false and combines them with NOT, AND, OR, implication, and equivalence. A knowledge base is a set of sentences; entailment asks whether every model that satisfies the knowledge base also satisfies a query.
examples:
rain=True
umbrella=True
print("protected from rain:", (not rain) or umbrella)
lessons.example:
rain=True; umbrella=True
print("protected from rain:", (not rain) or umbrella)
commonMistakes: Treating implication P→Q as if it also means Q→P is the classic converse error and produces invalid conclusions.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Logical inference, entailment & resolution
objectives: Derive conclusions using sound inference rather than intuition.
Explain how entailment changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect entailment with resolution and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Inference algorithms transform or inspect a knowledge base to prove consequences. Resolution works conveniently with clauses in conjunctive normal form and proves a query by showing that adding its negation leads to contradiction.
lessons.explain: Inference algorithms transform or inspect a knowledge base to prove consequences. Resolution works conveniently with clauses in conjunctive normal form and proves a query by showing that adding its negation leads to contradiction.
lessons.example:
facts={"cloudy", "cloudy->rain"}
if "cloudy" in facts and "cloudy->rain" in facts: print("derive: rain")
commonMistakes: Using a plausible real-world belief that was never encoded in the knowledge base is not logical inference from the represented facts.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: First-order logic & unification
objectives: Represent objects, relations, variables, and quantified rules.
Explain how first-order logic changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect first-order logic with predicate and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: First-order logic extends propositional logic with objects, predicates, functions, variables, and quantifiers. Instead of a separate proposition for every person, a rule can state that all humans satisfy some property.
lessons.explain: First-order logic extends propositional logic with objects, predicates, functions, variables, and quantifiers. Instead of a separate proposition for every person, a rule can state that all humans satisfy some property.
commonMistakes: Confusing existential “there exists” with universal “for all” changes the meaning of a rule completely.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Knowledge representation: rules, frames & ontologies
objectives: Choose a representation that exposes the relationships an inference task needs.
Explain how knowledge representation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect knowledge representation with ontology and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Knowledge representation is the engineering decision about how concepts, categories, attributes, relations, defaults, and rules are encoded. Rule systems are good for explicit implications, graph/ontology representations are good for typed entities and relationships, and structured frames can group properties around concepts.
lessons.explain: Knowledge representation is the engineering decision about how concepts, categories, attributes, relations, defaults, and rules are encoded. Rule systems are good for explicit implications, graph/ontology representations are good for typed entities and relationships, and structured frames can group properties around concepts.
commonMistakes: A representation that stores facts but cannot express the relationships needed by the reasoning task forces complex, brittle application code later.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Reasoning under uncertainty & Bayes networks
objectives: Represent uncertain dependencies and update beliefs from evidence.
Explain how Bayes network changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Bayes network with conditional probability and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Real environments rarely provide complete certainty. Bayesian networks represent random variables as a directed acyclic graph whose edges capture conditional dependencies; local conditional probability tables define the joint distribution compactly when independences hold.
lessons.explain: Real environments rarely provide complete certainty. Bayesian networks represent random variables as a directed acyclic graph whose edges capture conditional dependencies; local conditional probability tables define the joint distribution compactly when independences hold.
examples:
prior=0.01
sensitivity=0.9
false_positive=0.05
p_pos=prior*sensitivity + (1-prior)*false_positive
posterior=prior*sensitivity/p_pos
print(round(posterior,3))
lessons.example:
prior=0.01; sensitivity=0.9; false_positive=0.05
p_pos=prior*sensitivity + (1-prior)*false_positive
posterior=prior*sensitivity/p_pos
print(round(posterior,3))
commonMistakes: Interpreting P(test positive | disease) as P(disease | test positive) ignores the base rate and is a common probabilistic reasoning error.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Planning with actions, preconditions & effects
objectives: Represent a goal-directed plan as actions that transform symbolic state.
Explain how planning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect planning with precondition and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Classical planning separates action definitions from the specific problem instance. An action has preconditions that must be true before it can execute and effects that change the state.
lessons.explain: Classical planning separates action definitions from the specific problem instance. An action has preconditions that must be true before it can execute and effects that change the state.
commonMistakes: Allowing an action to execute without checking its preconditions creates impossible plans that look valid only because state transitions were under-specified.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Plan-space, hierarchical & partial-order planning
objectives: Reason about plans without forcing every action into a fixed total order too early.
Explain how partial-order planning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect partial-order planning with hierarchical planning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Some planning problems are easier when the system commits only to ordering constraints that are necessary. Partial-order planning can leave independent actions unordered, while hierarchical planning decomposes abstract tasks into smaller methods and actions.
lessons.explain: Some planning problems are easier when the system commits only to ordering constraints that are necessary. Partial-order planning can leave independent actions unordered, while hierarchical planning decomposes abstract tasks into smaller methods and actions.
commonMistakes: Imposing an arbitrary total order on independent tasks can remove concurrency and expand the search space without improving correctness.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Markov Decision Processes as a bridge to RL
objectives: Model sequential decisions where actions have uncertain outcomes.
Explain how MDP changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MDP with transition probability and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A Markov Decision Process specifies states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and a discount factor. Unlike deterministic planning, an action may lead to several next states with different probabilities.
lessons.explain: A Markov Decision Process specifies states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and a discount factor. Unlike deterministic planning, an action may lead to several next states with different probabilities.
commonMistakes: Choosing the action with the largest immediate reward can be worse over time when it leads to poor future states.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Choosing the right AI formulation & evaluating search
objectives: Select search, CSP, logic, planning, probability, or learning based on problem structure.
Explain how problem formulation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect problem formulation with baseline and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Near-mastery is the ability to recognize the structure before reaching for an algorithm. If you need a path, use search; if you need a consistent assignment, consider CSP; if you need provable symbolic consequences, use logic; if actions achieve symbolic goals, use planning; if uncertainty matters, use probabilistic models or MDPs.
lessons.explain: Near-mastery is the ability to recognize the structure before reaching for an algorithm. If you need a path, use search; if you need a consistent assignment, consider CSP; if you need provable symbolic consequences, use logic; if actions achieve symbolic goals, use planning; if uncertainty matters, use probabilistic models or MDPs.
commonMistakes: Picking an algorithm because it is advanced or fashionable instead of because its assumptions match the problem often creates unnecessary complexity.
